article.title: How to Seal Grout in a Shower or Bathroom Floor
article.summary: Seal tile grout to block stains and mildew: deep-clean the joints, let them dry, apply a penetrating sealer, wipe the excess and test with water.
article.body:
Cement grout is porous, so it soaks up soap, dirt and water, which leads to stains and mildew. A penetrating sealer fills those pores. This guide covers sanded and unsanded cement grout in showers, backsplashes and floors.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: run the bathroom fan and open a window. Wear nitrile gloves. Never mix bleach cleaners with ammonia or acidic cleaners.

Steps

  1. Check whether your grout needs sealing

    Drip a few drops of water on several grout lines. If the grout darkens within a few minutes, it's absorbing water and needs sealer. If the water beads up, the existing sealer is still working. Epoxy and urethane grouts don't need sealing at all.

    Done right: you know which areas absorb water, usually the shower floor and the lower walls.

  2. Wait for new grout to cure

    New grout needs to cure before sealing. Many grout makers say 48 to 72 hours; check your grout bag. On older grout, repair any cracked or crumbling joints first, because sealer doesn't fill gaps.

    Done right: the grout is fully cured and every joint is intact.

  3. Deep-clean the grout lines

    Scrub the joints with a pH-neutral cleaner and a stiff nylon brush. For dark stains or mildew, use an oxygen bleach solution, let it sit 10 minutes, scrub, and rinse well with clean water. Sealing over dirt locks it in.

    Done right: the grout is an even color with no gray film or spots.

  4. Let it dry completely

    Run the fan and don't use the shower for at least 24 hours, or as long as the sealer label says. Water trapped under the sealer can cause a cloudy look and weak protection.

    Done right: the grout looks uniformly light and dry, with no darker damp patches.

  5. Apply the sealer to the joints

    Work in sections of a few square feet. Run an applicator-tip bottle or small foam brush along each grout line, putting the sealer on the grout rather than across the tile. Let it soak in for the time on the label, usually 5 to 15 minutes, then wipe any sealer off the tile faces with a clean microfiber cloth before it dries. Apply a second coat if the label calls for it.

    Done right: there is no sticky or hazy film on the tile surface.

  6. Let it cure and test

    Keep water off for the full cure time on the label, often 24 to 72 hours. Then repeat the water-drop test on the same spots you tested at the start.

    Done right: water beads up on the grout and wipes away without darkening it.

Call a tile pro if: grout is cracked or missing in a shower, tiles sound hollow when tapped, or the wall behind the tile feels soft. Those point to water behind the tile, and sealer won't fix it.

FAQ

How often should you seal grout?

It depends on use and the sealer, but many sealers last 1 to 3 years. Do the water-drop test every few months on the shower floor, which wears fastest.

Can you seal old grout?

Yes, once it's deep-cleaned and fully dry. Repair cracked joints first.

Does grout sealer prevent mold?

It slows it down by keeping water and soap out of the grout, but it doesn't make grout mold-proof. Good ventilation matters just as much.

What happens if sealer dries on the tile?

It leaves a hazy film. Most manufacturers sell a remover, or you can rub it off with more sealer and a cloth while it's still fresh.
